The feature was officially previewed with GPT-5.6 Sol. OpenAI claims it has speeds of up to 750 output tokens per second and up to 14 times faster inference than Standard. The mode is powered by Cerebras. Access remains limited to select customers.

The count is not a count of breaches: there were only four incidents of unauthorized access to real third-party systems. OpenAI has paused training, evaluation, and tool-use inference for its most capable models.

articles.headline: Can AI self-improvement overcome diminishing returns?
articles.blurb: AI is already helping build better AI. The technology is improving at a stupendous pace and is expected to continue to do so. Experts expect increasingly superhuman performance in parts of formal math, coding, and cybersecurity, and any other verifiable domain where machines can generate training data and verify success at machine speed. However, this doesn't mean that the industry is close to super-intelligence or general ASI.

articles.headline: Agent (Muse) Compute Demand
articles.blurb: It costs Meta an estimated around 1 to 2 gigawatts of average total power to serve 100 million daily active users. Only around 0.1 gigawatts comes from the GPU/VM layer. 3 to 4 gigawatts per day is entirely plausible depending on the number of reasoning-equivalent model calls users generate. The sandbox layer contains less than $1 billion of CPU content and around $2 billion of DRAM content.

articles.headline: Claude computes a nine-loop amplitude in N=4 super-Yang-Mills
articles.blurb: Physicists at Anthropic harnessed Claude, an LLM, to compute a complex nine-loop amplitude in N=4 super-Yang-Mills, a problem once considered computationally infeasible with limited resources. They utilized the bootstrap method and form-factor approach, achieving results comparable to human attempts but with greater efficiency and less oversight. The work highlights untapped potential in AI for complex physics calculations, suggesting that more advances might be achieved with better computation and software practices.

articles.headline: Hitting a billion tokens per minute on one GPU by combining a query planner and an inference engine
articles.blurb: The QUery-Aware Inference Layer (Quail) is an inference engine that hits over a billion tokens processed per minute per H100 GPU. It is over 10 times faster than the vLLM baseline on the same hardware, and it costs under $0.06 per billion tokens on Modal. This post provides a quick overview of how Quail works. It focuses more on considerations for inference engineers.

articles.headline: On Ezra Klein's Podcast With Jensen Huang
articles.blurb: Jensen Huang doesn't believe in superintelligence or that AI will ever be a different kind of thing from software. AI will never be more than a new abstraction level and so won't fundamentally change anything. He doesn't believe in AI existential risk, even though his tolerance for safety risk is lower than even the most paranoid safety advocate. Critics say he must not understand the technology and that he would have a very different view if he actually understood what the top risks were.

articles.blurb: OpenAI claims one of its agentic AI systems trained in what was supposed to be a secured, internet-free environment was able to gain access to the web to reach an external third-party chatbot. The agent apparently exploited a gap to reach the public internet to send 20 queries to an unnamed, third-party chatbot service. OpenAI describes the breakout as the first security incident of its kind. The company has stopped training the model, but said it provided an important signal about where to focus the next phase of work.

articles.headline: Meta's VR Glasses Are What the Apple Vision Pro Should Have Been
articles.blurb: Apple's Vision Pro has not sold well, and the company has since decided to redirect resources to other products. Meta's new VR glasses use a similar design that offloads the computing engine, allowing the device to weigh one-sixth as much as the Vision Pro - at one-third of the price. This article offers a look at what the new Meta VR Glasses experience is like compared to the Vision Pro. For a device that won't launch until next Spring, the experience is surprisingly refined, and the glasses improve on the Vision Pro in several ways.

articles.headline: Waymo's Latest Safety Numbers Sure Make Human Drivers Look Bad
articles.blurb: Waymo reports 82% fewer injury-causing crashes than human drivers. The company has released data collected from over 270 million miles of fully autonomous driving. Waymo cars were involved in 95% fewer collisions that caused serious injury or worse, and there were 93% fewer pedestrian incidents that resulted in injuries compared to human drivers. While the company's data only measure the five metropolitan areas where it operated during the study period, it shows that the company's driverless robotaxis crash far less frequently than humans.

articles.headline: SpaceX's Starship Is Set to Make Its First Orbital Flight
articles.blurb: SpaceX is aiming to reach orbit on Starship's 14th test flight. The test flight is scheduled for Monday at around 8 AM ET, with SpaceX providing live coverage of the event on its website. Achieving orbital flight will allow Starship to deploy satellites and travel to more distant destinations. SpaceX will not try to catch the two rocket stages during the test - the booster will make a simulated landing in the Gulf of Mexico, and the upper stage will simulate a landing in the Pacific Ocean to the west of Chile.

articles.headline: Do my hard-won product skills still matter in the AI era?
articles.blurb: AI made building software much cheaper, which puts the hard parts of product work in sharper focus. Judgment, craft, and understanding your customer still move at human speed. The role of product management is shifting from deciding what's worth building to deciding what's worth shipping. Product management isn't dead, and it isn't optional.

articles.headline: S3 Is the Future, S3 Is the Past
articles.blurb: Since S3's release 20 years ago, SSD prices have dropped steadily, and the gap between SSD and disk has narrowed to roughly 3x. S3-based infrastructure has now become the industry standard. However, the hardware constraints that motivated it are fading. The industry is codifying architectural patterns that exist to work around limitations that SSD storage doesn't have. Cloud providers have no incentive to disrupt a model that serves them well, so developers need to build the infrastructure primitives themselves.

articles.headline: Tesla workers balk at training Optimus humanoid robots as replacements
articles.blurb: The complexity of Optimus' hands has translated to more production headaches for Tesla, as human workers must manually assemble the hands and forearms together using more than 100 small components. The heavy reliance on imitation learning prompted Tesla to have factory workers wear special suits designed to record their physical movements while working. Some workers complained as they knew they were training robots to eventually replace them. Tesla has since shifted data collection to dedicated teams.

The agent was also referenced as a benefit on the upgrade page for the $100 Pro plan. An always-on agent would fit OpenAI's broader move from conversational interfaces to software that can carry out longer-running work with less supervision.

A deal would give Nubank an immediate UK and European banking foothold through Monzo's 16 million customers and £1.7 billion of annual revenue, while likely ending Monzo's near-term path to a standalone IPO.

articles.headline: ACH use rises for B2B payments
articles.blurb: ACH has overtaken checks as the most common US B2B payment method by transaction count, rising from 25% of payments in 2015 to 41% in 2024 while checks fell from 32% to 13%. ACH transaction value nearly doubled to $70 trillion over the period, though wires still dominate by value at roughly $1 quadrillion, showing that businesses are steadily shifting routine payments toward electronic rails even as checks remain widely used.

articles.headline: Agent Wars: Amazon vs. Muse
articles.blurb: Simon Taylor argues that Amazon's decision to block Meta's Muse agent is an early battle over who owns the customer, captures commerce fees, and bears liability when AI agents transact on users' behalf. He expects the key infrastructure layer to be “Know Your Agent” standards that authenticate agents, define delegated authority, and allocate liability, with merchants, wallets, card networks, platforms, and infrastructure providers all competing to control that trust layer.

articles.headline: UK banks pilot tokenised deposit transactions
articles.blurb: UK banks have collaborated to complete the first live customer transactions using tokenised sterling deposits. The transactions were delivered through the Great British Tokenised Deposit (GBTD) initiative, which was convened by UK Finance and involves Barclays, HSBC UK, Lloyds Banking Group, Monzo, Nationwide, NatWest, and Santander.

articles.headline: Numeral raises $100M Series C to expand AI-powered tax compliance
articles.blurb: Numeral raised a $100 million Series C led by Insight Partners, bringing total funding to $157 million as it expands its AI-powered sales tax compliance platform across software, manufacturing, distribution, and wholesale. The company says transaction volume is up 327% year over year and is positioning itself as end-to-end tax infrastructure spanning nexus monitoring, registrations, calculation, filings, remittance, and exemption certificates, with support for VAT and GST in more than 90 countries.

articles.headline: SEC clarifies that certain staked Ethereum receipt tokens are not securities
articles.blurb: SEC staff clarified that liquid-staking receipt tokens tied to non-security crypto assets like ETH generally are not securities when they simply represent ownership of the underlying staked asset and do not add separate rights, returns, or managerial promises. The guidance builds on the SEC's earlier position on liquid staking, but remains staff guidance rather than binding law, meaning its treatment could change through future rulemaking, legislation, or a different administration.

articles.headline: Data Broker Radaris Loses Domains in Privacy Fight
articles.blurb: The consumer data broker Radaris.com has long had a reputation for ignoring requests to remove personal information from its vast empire of people-search services online. That reputation caught up with the company recently in a lawsuit alleging Radaris violated a New Jersey privacy law that provides for hefty fines against data brokers that publish personal information on state law enforcement officials. In the face of repeated stonewalling and prevarication by attorneys for Radaris, the judge in the case ordered that radaris.com and more than a dozen other data broker domains be transferred to the plaintiffs.

articles.headline: Microsoft Plugs Nearly 1,000 Security Holes
articles.blurb: Microsoft Corp. today issued updates to plug at least 974 security holes in its Windows operating systems and other software, by far its biggest single patch batch ever. Microsoft says artificial intelligence is helping to speed the discovery of vulnerabilities, but security experts warn that many organizations already are struggling to prioritize the more human-intensive endeavor of testing and deploying so many fixes each month.

articles.headline: FBI Probes Service Selling 153M+ Drivers Licenses
articles.blurb: A new identity theft service launched on the dark web this week is selling digital scans of more than 153 million drivers licenses from people in the United States and Canada. Based on interviews with individuals whose licenses are available for purchase on this service, it appears to be siphoning images collected by a widely-used identity verification company based in Louisiana. KrebsOnSecurity also has learned that the New Orleans field office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) today launched an official inquiry into the source of the images.

articles.headline: Two Alleged ‘TeamPCP’ Hackers Arrested in Australia
articles.blurb: Authorities in Australia have arrested two men believed to be members of TeamPCP, a prolific cybercrime and data extortion group blamed for perpetrating the longest running spree of software supply chain attacks ever. In a statement released today, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) said two unnamed suspects from Western Australia, aged 21 and 23, were arrested in connection with a "sophisticated cybercrime syndicate that allegedly created malicious open-source software to rob thousands of global businesses." The AFP did not name the defendants, but KrebsOnSecurity learned the 21-year-old suspect's real identity in June, and has been communicating with him ever since. This story includes interviews with TeamPCP's self-described spokesperson, and examines clues left behind by the TeamPCP leader that likely led to his undoing.

articles.headline: Who’s Tracking You? Use This New Service to Find Out
articles.blurb: It can be daunting to determine who's responsible for showing ads on the websites we visit, or who's harvesting data from the mobile apps we use every day. That information is already semi-public, but it is not easily parsed and traditionally much of it has remained walled away in the hands of large advertising platforms. Not anymore: A powerful and free new service called DecryptAds scrapes and correlates this adtech data and makes it simple to quickly learn a great deal about the entities that are tracking you.

articles.headline: Microsoft Plugs Nearly 400 Security Holes

articles.headline: Canadian Man Pleads Guilty in Snowflake Extortions
articles.blurb: A 26-year-old Canadian man once described as one of the most consequential cybercrime threat actors of 2024 has pleaded guilty to computer fraud and conspiracy to hack and extort more than 165 organizations that used the cloud data storage provider Snowflake. Connor Riley Moucka, of Kitchener, Ontario, also admitted to stealing call and text history records of more than 100 million AT&T customers.

articles.headline: Read This Before You Buy That TV Streaming Stick
articles.blurb: Security experts have been sounding the alarm for years about the risks of using generic TV boxes that promise unlimited content streaming for a one-time fee, warning that they secretly rent the user's Internet connection out to strangers. But a groundbreaking new analysis finds these devices also routinely spoof themselves as mobile phones clicking ads on AI-generated websites as part of sprawling operation that seeks to defraud online merchants and advertising networks.
